opus-5.5.text:
I think we have to be careful about treating human annotations as a gold standard. They're incredibly valuable, and for a long time the whole field has been built on that assumption, but when you actually look closely at annotated datasets, you find a lot of noise. Humans get tired, instructions get interpreted differently by different annotators, boundaries on segmentation masks are drawn loosely, rare classes get mislabeled, and sometimes the ontology itself is ambiguous. So what we call "ground truth" is really more like "human consensus under particular constraints."

In some of the work we've been doing, we compared labels generated automatically by foundation models against human labels, and what was striking is that in a good number of cases where the two disagreed, the automatic label was arguably the correct one, or at least just as defensible. That doesn't mean you throw humans out of the loop. It means the role of the human shifts. Instead of labeling everything from scratch, people become reviewers and adjudicators. They focus on the hard cases, the ambiguous ones, and the ones where the model is uncertain.

So my view is that human annotations are a reference point, not an infallible standard. If you evaluate auto-labeling purely against human labels, you'll sometimes penalize the model for being right. A better approach is to measure agreement, look at where the disagreements are, and actually inspect them, and ultimately to judge the labels by what matters downstream: does a model trained on these labels perform well on the task you care about? That's the real test.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I'd push back a little on the framing of "gold standard." I think the field has treated human annotation as ground truth for a long time, and that's been enormously productive, but we should be honest about what it actually is. It's a measurement. It's a noisy, context-dependent measurement of what a particular person, under particular instructions, with a particular amount of time and attention, decided to write down about an image.

So when you look closely at any large labeled dataset, you find a lot of disagreement. You give the same image to five annotators and ask them to name the objects, and you'll get overlap, sure, but you'll also get real variation. One person says "dog," another says "golden retriever," another says "pet." One person labels the chair in the background, another doesn't bother because it wasn't salient to them. And none of those people are wrong, exactly. They're just answering slightly different questions than the one you thought you asked.

What that means for evaluation is that when your automatic labeler disagrees with the human annotation, you can't immediately say the machine made an error. Sometimes it did. Sometimes the human missed something. And sometimes the "disagreement" is really a vocabulary mismatch or a granularity mismatch, and the metric is punishing you for a difference that doesn't matter semantically. So I like to think of the human labels as a reference distribution rather than a single correct answer. If you can get multiple annotators, the agreement among them tells you something important: it tells you the ceiling. If humans only agree with each other eighty percent of the time on some category, then a system hitting ninety-five against one annotator is probably just overfitting to that annotator's idiosyncrasies, not actually doing better than people.

The other thing I'd say is that annotations are shaped by the task design. The instructions you give, the interface, whether you pay per image or per hour, all of that leaks into the data. So the gold standard is really encoding a bunch of experimental choices that often get forgotten by the time the dataset becomes a benchmark that everyone cites. I think we'd be better off if we treated the annotation process itself as something to study and report, rather than hiding it behind the word "ground truth."

So, useful? Absolutely. Necessary? Probably, at least for now. But gold standard implies a kind of certainty that I don't think the data actually supports, and that gap matters more and more as the systems get closer to human-level performance, because that's exactly where the noise in the labels starts to dominate what you're measuring.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to be careful about calling human annotations a gold standard. They're a useful reference, but an annotation is a person's interpretation of an image, and that interpretation depends on the task, the instructions, and what that person happens to notice. Two people can look at the same image and give different labels without either of them necessarily being wrong.

So when an automatic label disagrees with a human annotation, that tells us there's a disagreement; it doesn't, by itself, establish that the machine made a mistake. We need to understand how consistently humans can do the task and how much ambiguity there is in the labels. I'd treat human annotations as measurements with uncertainty, rather than as an unquestionable definition of what's in the image.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about calling human annotations a gold standard. They’re a useful reference, but they’re still measurements made by people, and people bring different interpretations to an image. They may disagree about what’s present, which objects matter, or how specific a label should be.

If one person labels an image “dog” and another labels it “Labrador,” that isn’t necessarily a disagreement about the visual content. And if an automatic system produces a valid label that the annotator didn’t include, we shouldn’t automatically count that as an error.

So I’d want multiple annotations, some understanding of agreement between annotators, and clear instructions about the task. Human labels are essential, but treating them as unquestionable truth can hide both annotation errors and legitimate differences in interpretation.
